questions.question: A 32-layer fixture has 4,096-by-4,096 query and value projections. If LoRA rank is 16 on both projections, how many trainable adapter parameters are added?
questions.explanation: Each projection adds r(d_in + d_out) = 16(4,096 + 4,096) parameters. Multiply by two projections and 32 layers to get 8,388,608.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a LoRA adapter artifact?
options: It is a complete model that can load on any checkpoint with the same hidden size
It is portable whenever the rank matches
It replaces the need to version the tokenizer and chat template
It is a delta tied to an exact base-model and input-format contract
questions.explanation: The learned update depends on the base weights and the token sequence used during training. Base revision, tokenizer, template, target modules, and adapter configuration are part of correctness.

questions.question: A rank-16 run underperforms on a rare slice. What is the sound next decision?
options: Check data coverage, target modules, and held-out behavior before increasing rank
Set rank to the maximum because more parameters guarantee quality
Remove the rare slice from the release gate
Merge the adapter so the missing behavior appears
questions.explanation: Underperformance may come from missing examples, the wrong adaptation surface, or optimization. Rank is only one hypothesis and larger adapters do not guarantee better generalization.

questions.question: What resource does QLoRA primarily reduce compared with LoRA over BF16 or FP16 base weights?
options: The number of prompt tokens
The need for held-out evaluation
The storage memory for the frozen base weights
The adapter's dependence on a base revision
questions.explanation: QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit form while training higher-precision LoRA parameters. Activation memory, evaluation, and compatibility requirements remain.

questions.question: Under original LoRA scaling, rank increases from 16 to 32 while alpha stays 32. What happens to alpha divided by rank?
options: It doubles from 2 to 4
It halves from 2 to 1
It stays at 2
It becomes zero
questions.explanation: Original LoRA scales the update by alpha/r. With alpha fixed at 32, the factor changes from 32/16 = 2 to 32/32 = 1.

questions.question: A merged checkpoint loads without an adapter-capable runtime. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The merge proves held-out task and safety quality
The merged model no longer needs tokenizer or template lineage
Rollback is unnecessary because there is only one artifact
The merged artifact still needs lineage, evaluation, integrity, and rollback gates
questions.explanation: Merging changes packaging and can simplify inference. It does not prove model quality or remove the need to identify, evaluate, sign, and roll back the resulting full checkpoint.

questions.question: Training loss falls while validation loss and a critical slice both worsen. What should the release process do?
options: Deploy the last checkpoint because it minimized training loss
Increase the learning rate until validation follows training
Hold release, inspect earlier checkpoints and data leakage, and reduce optimization pressure
Switch from dynamic loading to a merged artifact
questions.explanation: Diverging held-out evidence is an overfitting or data-quality signal. Checkpoint selection and remediation must use validation and slice results, not training loss alone.

questions.question: Why does a common LoRA initialization set one factor to zero?
options: So the initial low-rank update is zero and wrapping the base starts as a no-op
So both factors remain frozen for the entire run
So alpha is no longer needed
So every target matrix has full rank
questions.explanation: If B starts at zero, BA is zero at initialization. The adapter initially preserves the base output while gradients can still begin learning the update.
